newsitem.title: FRANCE: Aero-engine market healthy but tough, says GE.
newsitem.headline: Aero-engine market healthy but tough, says GE.

text.p: The world aero-engine market is seeing healthy orders but tough pricing demands from customers and high development costs are keeping the pressure on, GE Aircraft Engines said on Tuesday.

Sales for engine companies slumped along with the rest of the aerospace industry after airlines flew into a recession in the early and mid-1990s. Order cancellations hit engine and aircraft makers and their suppliers hard.

Although world travel has picked up again, airlines and plane makers Airbus Industrie and Boeing Co are cutting tough deals on the engines, which make up around a third of the cost buying a passenger jet.

"The industry recovery is well under way," Eugene Murphy, president and chief executive officer of General Electric Aircraft Engines told reporters at the Paris air show on Tuesday. The company is a unit of U.S. General Electric.
"The industry is under a lot of cost pressure," he added.
GE expects to deliver around 1,900 engines this year, compared with 1,800 in 1996, either directly or through its marketing joint venture with French state-owned Snecma, briefing documents showed.

The engine company had 1996 turnover of $6.3 billion and operating profit of $1.23 billion, giving a ratio of profit to sales of 19.4 percent. Murphy said it looked for a return on investment of between 13 to 15 percent as "a threshold level".

GE decided not to supply engines for derivatives of Airbus's A340 long-haul jet, the A340-500 and A340-600 which were launched earlier at the air show at Le Bourget airport. "We were not able to come togther on the business terms," Murphy said.

Developing a new engine would have cost between $800 million and $1 billion and GE was unable to see the business case for the estimated 500 sales of the new aircraft, he said. But GE is still studying an engine in that category, developing 56,000 pounds of thrust.
GE has also decided not to build more powerful versions of its GE90 engine, which cost $1.5 billion to develop and powers the Boeing 777 giant twinjet.

It balked at the additional investment required to increase power from the current 92,000 pounds to above 100,000 pounds, given the need to generate a return on investment, he said. The more powerful motor would be used to power Boeing's planned heavyweight derivatives of its 777-200 and 777-300 jets.
But GE is marketing the lower-thrust GE90 and expects to sign a major order by the end of the year, Murphy said.

Besides growth in civil and military engine sales, GE's acquisition of aircraft service companies Greenwich and UNC will help it to diversify into the overhaul and maintenance business. "This is truly a major strategic step," Murphy said. Combined annual sales of Greenwich and UNC were $1.8 billion.
GE has undertaken a productivity plan, in response to demands for cost reductions, which is expected to show $50 million in benefits this year and $500 million by 2000, when completed, Murphy said.
